claims.text: Corrosion resistance in steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily governed by formation of a stable protective oxide layer.
The protective oxide layer is enriched in chromium and other alloying elements.
The protective oxide layer inhibits further oxidation and chemical attack.
Exposure of chromium-containing steel to the proposed corrosive environments produces a chromium-rich surface oxide layer.
Chromium in steel reacts with environmental oxygen to form an oxide layer.
The chromium-containing oxide layer is dense and adherent.
The dense, adherent oxide acts as a barrier to further oxidation and chemical attack.
Steels with higher chromium content will have significantly lower corrosion rates than lower-chromium steels under identical conditions.
Plain carbon steels or other steels with minimal chromium provide the lower-chromium corrosion-rate baseline.
The hypothesis should hold for steels containing more than 10% chromium.
The hypothesis applies only where the protective oxide remains stable.
Temperatures below the oxide melting point are an example of conditions in which the oxide layer remains stable.
Aggressive reducing agents may make the hypothesis inapplicable.
Extremely high temperatures may destabilize the protective oxide layer.
Mechanical abrasion may destabilize or remove the protective oxide layer.
A controlled study will compare nominal 5%, 10%, and 15% chromium steels exposed to sulfuric-acid solutions at different concentrations and temperatures.
Corrosion will be evaluated by weight loss and electrochemical techniques, while oxide composition, thickness, and morphology will be characterized by diffraction and microscopy.
Failure of higher-chromium steels to show significantly lower corrosion rates or to form a stable protective oxide under the tested conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
